text.hook:
"string_view is just a faster const std::string&."
It is a pointer and a length. Every rule follows from that.

The mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Swipe ➜ and save it.
text.body:
Inside:
1. What a view is made of
2. Views that dangle at the semicolon
3. `data()` and C APIs
4. Choosing a text parameter, and `std::span`
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: A pointer and a length. Every rule follows from that.

slides.title: A borrow with no borrow checker

cards.label: span<T> (C++20)
cards.text: `{T* data; size_t size;}` over any contiguous `T`.

cards.label: Never
cards.text: Allocates, frees, or extends any lifetime.

slides.takeaway: Great parameters. Risky return values, members, map keys and captured lambda state.

slides.title: Views that dangle at the semicolon
rows: Safe: `g` takes a view and does not store it
slides.takeaway: Lifetime extension needs a reference. A `string_view` is an object: binding it to a temporary extends nothing.

slides.lead: A view from `substr` or `(ptr, len)` usually has no terminator. `strlen`, `printf("%s")`, `fopen` read past it. `std::cout << sv` is fine: it uses the size.

cards.label: `s[i] = c`
cards.text: Valid: same memory, the view sees the write.

cards.label: `s += ...`, `clear()`
cards.text: Formally invalid, even without reallocation. The view's size never updates.

slides.title: Which type for text?
rows: Read only, during the call, no terminator needed
slides.takeaway: A view parameter does not stop the function from storing the view. Storing needs an owning copy.

slides.title: Static or dynamic extent

cards.label: `span<int, 4>`
cards.text: Size in the type, only a pointer: 8 bytes.

slides.takeaway: A `std::span<const T>` parameter accepts a vector, a `std::array` or a C array: no template, no copy.

items.truth: It owns nothing and extends nothing.

items.myth: "A view of a returned temporary lives until the caller's statement ends."
items.truth: `return std::string("x");` as a view dies at the end of that `return`, inside the callee.

items.myth: "If the string does not reallocate, my view is still valid."
items.truth: Any non-exempt mutation formally invalidates it, and its size never updates.

items.myth: "A `string_view` can modify the characters it views."
items.truth: It is read-only. `std::span<char>` can write through.
Not if the function needs `c_str()`: the view forces a copy later.

slides.hero:
A view is exactly
as valid as
its owner.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Slice a record into a string_view.
One line, no copy, no warning from GCC.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The kind of line that ships in a parser refactor.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `record.substr(...)` is `std::string::substr`: a new owning string, not a view of `record`.
The view binds to that temporary, which dies at the semicolon.
The 30-char substring lives on the heap, so the print reads freed memory.
A short substring sits in the SSO buffer and may print correctly: still UB.
slides.wrong: "Prints the identifier: string_view slices are zero-copy"

slides.title: Make the view first, then slice
slides.tip: Clang warns here with `-Wdangling-gsl`. GCC 11 with `-Wall -Wextra` is silent.

text.hook:
`use_default` is false.
So `label` just views `configured`. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: No threads, no heap tricks. One conditional operator.

slides.title:
Run with no arguments.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: Even on the false branch. ASan: `heap-use-after-free`
bullets: `?:` needs one type for both branches: `const char[8]` and `std::string` give a `std::string` prvalue.
So the expression makes a **temporary copy** of `configured`.
The view binds to the copy, which dies at the semicolon. It never pointed at `configured`.
slides.wrong: "Prints the configured name: the false branch is just `configured`"

slides.title: Make both branches views
slides.tip: Now the common type is `std::string_view`: no temporary, no copy.
slides.takeaway: The conditional operator's type can be an owning temporary.

text.hook:
A 3-character view of "abcdef".
Hand its `data()` to `strlen`. What comes back?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Every C API boundary in your codebase asks this question.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `strlen(v.data())` scans for `'\0'`, which only comes after `"def"` in `t`'s buffer: 6.
The scan stays inside `t`, so it is not UB, just wrong. A view into a raw buffer may have no terminator at all.

slides.title: Pass the size, or a terminated copy
slides.code:
std::printf("%.*s\n", int(v.size()),
            v.data());       // abc

std::string owned(v);  // copy + '\0'
std::puts(owned.c_str());     // abc
slides.tip: Functions that forward to C APIs should take `const std::string&`, not a view.
slides.takeaway: Never hand `string_view::data()` to an API that expects a null-terminated string.

text.hook:
A span over a vector with spare capacity.
push_back, then write `v[0]`.
What does the span see?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: `reserve` runs before the span is made. That detail matters.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `reserve(10)` ran before the span was made, so `push_back` keeps the same block.
The span stored `(data(), 3)` at construction: its size stays 3.
`v[0] = 100` writes the shared memory, so `s[0]` sees 100.
slides.wrong: "`4 100 4`: the span is a live view of the vector"

slides.title: Drop the `reserve`
slides.code:
std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};  // cap 3
std::span<int> s = v;
v.push_back(4);  // reallocates
std::cout << s[0];  // UB: freed memory
slides.tip: libstdc++ grows capacity 3 to 6 here. ASan: `heap-use-after-free` on `s[0]`.
slides.takeaway: A span shares elements, never size changes, and dies on reallocation.
